source.title: A suite of Vision Sparse Autoencoders

record.tranche_reason: The study trains and provides sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool for a vision transformer, but does not test superposition, capacity pressure, or any of the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The post reports qualitative layer-wise auto-interpretability and activation-frequency findings, and reconstruction-MSE plots across image tokens. These do not test the listed versions: the model is a vision transformer, and the study does not test superposition geometry, capacity competition, or whether SAE features are complete or canonical. The MSE plots are not relevant to those claims.
record.test_reason: The post releases top-k SAEs trained on a CLIP vision transformer as a tool. Its only findings are qualitative layer comparisons (monosemanticity, activation frequency) and per-token reconstruction MSE. None measures superposition geometry, capacity competition, other causes of polysemanticity, distributed features in LLMs, SAE feature canonicality, or feature dimensionality.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors say the findings are preliminary and not rigorous. They suggest layer 20 is a reasonable alternative to layer 22. They also say outer image tokens were easier to reconstruct during training, which they attribute to those tokens carrying more important information.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains top-k sparse autoencoders on a vision transformer; it does not reproduce the toy-network superposition method or its measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported qualitative monosemanticity and activation-frequency comparisons vary by layer, with layer 20 described as highest.

fits_no_version.finding: In CLIP ViT-L SAEs, layer 20 is described as the most monosemantic under Sort Eval, and its features are said to activate most frequently on LAION. The comparison is qualitative and preliminary.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature interpretability and activation frequency vary across vision-transformer layers.

record.problems: The authors state that the analysis is preliminary and not demonstrated to a high degree of rigor. The layer comparison is qualitative, with no numerical scores or controls reported in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Reconstruction-MSE plots across image tokens were not recorded because they do not measure a listed claim version or a finding about superposition, capacity pressure, or SAE feature canonicality.

untested.parts: No toy models, feature overlap, orthogonality, or sparsity-dependent transition.
No test of capacity pressure or of dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
The subject is a vision transformer, not an LLM. No test of whether SAE recovery shows sparse features beyond the tool use itself.
No test of SAE feature completeness, stability across runs, or canonical status.
No test of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong post presenting a tool release (8 SAEs, 65536 features, k=32, on the residual stream). No numbers, controls or uncertainty are reported. Both rows correctly link to no version. The reconstruction-MSE omission is justified.

versions.untested_parts: No test of toy networks, feature overlap, orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
No test of capacity pressure, feature competition, or dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No test of alternative causes of polysemanticity or whether polysemanticity indicates superposition.
The study concerns a vision transformer, not an LLM, and does not test whether LLM features are distributed across neurons or recoverable as SAE features.
No test of SAE feature completeness, stability, or canonical status.
No test of whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.
